newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Red Cresent appeals for urgent aid.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Red Cresent appeals for urgent aid.

text.p: The head of Afghanistan's Red Cresent Society appealed on Thursday for urgent international aid for huge numbers of people in war-ravaged Kabul he said were in an "awful state".

"The people of Kabul are in an awful state and the aid given to them by foreign agencies is not sufficient," said Said Ahmad Ghafoori, President of the Afghan Red Crescent, the Moslem equivalent of the Red Cross.
"We ask the international community for urgent assistance for the people of Afghanistan and especially Kabul, whose people lead a grim life," he told reporters.

Western aid agencies reckon some 80 percent of Kabul's estimated one million people need food and other help as a bitter winter grips one of the world's most war-damaged cities, where huge swathes of buildings are in ruins.
The Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the United Nations and several Western aid groups are distributing food, but acknowledge their help is not enough.
There is food in the markets, but rapid inflation and widespread unemployment puts it out of reach of many, who cannot afford to buy fuel to cook what little food they have.

The plight of the city has worsened in the past two weeks as tens of thousands of refugees have poured into the city from the north, told to leave by the purist Islamist Taleban as they pushed back the forces of a northern alliance.
Many of the latest wave of Afghan refugees are effectively penniless. The only money they have was issued by northern Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The Taleban, who have taken control of two-thirds of Afghanistan and pushed the previous government out of Kabul in September, do not recognise "Dostum money".
There are more than 40,000 war widows in Kabul and widespread poverty has denied them traditional help from their extended families.
The ICRC helps around 30,000 war widows and the Red Crescent Society has been giving basic food and fuel supplied by Australia to a further 2,500.
Some of the thousands of people disabled in 18 years of war also get help.
Outside the Red Crescent office on Thursday, a long line of women -- clad in the all-enveloping burqa mandated by the Taleban -- waited chaotically for handouts.

But there was wailing from those not on the distribution list. One woman sobbed that her son was in hospital and his only hope was for her to get food aid and to sell it to buy medicines the doctors did not have.
She got nothing, because she was not on the list.
"We have lots of people who come and ask for help, but we suffer much more because of the shortage of aid" available for distribution, Ghafoori said.
"There is hunger in Kabul. About half the people have not eaten meat in months," he said. Meat, mostly goat, and unleavened bread are Afghanistan's staples.
"People live off tea and bread," he said.
